title: Linear Momentum
short: Momentum p = mv is a vector, and a system's momentum is the vector sum of its parts.
trouble: Students add momenta as plain numbers, forgetting that opposite directions cancel.

blocks.html: In Physical Science you met momentum as mass times velocity. Physics 1 adds one important idea: momentum is a vector. It points the way the object moves, so on a line it carries a sign, and in a plane it has components, just like the vectors you add by components.

Momentum is $\role{momentum}{\vec{p}} = \role{mass}{m}\role{velocity}{\vec{v}}$, measured in $\text{kg·m/s}$. On a line, pick a positive direction and give each momentum a sign. The momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of its parts: $\vec{p}_{\text{tot}} = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2 + \dots$

Why multiply mass by velocity? Because that product is what a force changes. Newton's second law says $F = ma = m\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, so $F\Delta t = \Delta(mv)$: a push lasting a while changes $mv$, whatever the mass. A loaded truck and a bicycle at the same speed are very different to stop, and $mv$ measures exactly that difference. Since velocity has a direction, so does $mv$, and two momenta in opposite directions cancel when you add them.

blocks.name: ph-collision

opts.task: Watch the momentum bars before the collision: $p_2$ points left, so it is a negative bar, and the total is a difference.

blocks.cap: Momentum bars for two gliders: each bar is $mv$ with a sign, and the teal bar is the total.

blocks.title: One object, with a sign
blocks.q: A $1200\ \text{kg}$ car drives west at $15\ \text{m/s}$. Taking east as positive, find its momentum.
steps: West is the negative direction, so $v = -15\ \text{m/s}$.
The size is $18{,}000\ \text{kg·m/s}$; the minus sign says "west".

blocks.title: Two objects on a line
blocks.q: Cart A ($2.0\ \text{kg}$) moves right at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$. Cart B ($4.0\ \text{kg}$) moves left at $1.0\ \text{m/s}$. Find the total momentum (right is positive).

blocks.title: Two objects at right angles
blocks.q: On ice, puck 1 ($0.20\ \text{kg}$) slides east at $6.0\ \text{m/s}$ and puck 2 ($0.20\ \text{kg}$) slides north at $8.0\ \text{m/s}$. How big is their total momentum?
steps: Adding the sizes ($2.8$) would be wrong because the momenta are not in the same direction.

blocks.html: Adding momenta as plain numbers. Two $3\ \text{kg·m/s}$ momenta can total $6$, $0$ or anything in between, depending on their directions. Before you add, write every velocity with its sign (or split it into components). Quick check: if two objects move toward each other, the total must be smaller than the bigger of the two momenta.

A small, fast object can carry as much momentum as a big, slow one: a $0.15\ \text{kg}$ baseball at $40\ \text{m/s}$ and a $6.0\ \text{kg}$ bowling ball at $1.0\ \text{m/s}$ both have $6.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$. Try collisions with momentum bars in the Momentum and Collisions lab of the Science Lab.
